title: PingFederate to Privilege: the OBO chain
lede: Simulated chain this lab walks: user SSO, RFC 8693 exchange (sub=user, act.sub=agent), Privilege NHI check, grant tiers, Cedar scope gate, Pass Agent Token backend. Steps mirror the eight scenarios.

nodes.label: MCP client
sub: signs in as a PF user

nodes.label: Non-Human Identity
sub: type OIDC Provider: iss, sub, JWKS

edges.label: tools/call with no token: 401, the door is its own authorization server
302 /authorize: scopes openid profile email offline_access p1:read:*
federates onward to the demo environment (one login)
Route A: PF added as an external OIDC IdP
PF authenticates the user; identity comes back, not PF claims
token issued by <tenant-a>; PF scopes are not expected in it
caller matched to a Privilege user by email alias; groups loaded
evaluate: context.app, Tool, context.args, context.token.scopes, principal in Group
allow, refuse (mcp:Invoke) or hold for a human (mcp:InvokeUnattended)
forwarded only when allowed; a hold waits for approval, then the client retries
route C: bearer = PF-issued JWT (untested on MCP)
verifies iss, sub, aud and signature against the registered JWKS; Resolved looks the person up
verified claims matched against RequiredClaims: any listed value per claim, every claim must match
only the matching tier's tools go on to Cedar, which still decides per tool

steps.title: User signs in at PingFederate
steps.what: The person signs in through PingFederate SSO; the client receives a subject token proving the user - and nothing else.
steps.why: The agent must never hold the user token; it only ever holds the OBO token minted for it.

steps.title: Sign-in is federated to the demo environment
steps.what: Environment <tenant-a> hands the sign-in on to <tenant-b>, the demo environment, so the user logs in once, there.
steps.why: That is the only place PingFederate can be added without touching Privilege.

steps.title: Route A: PingFederate as an external IdP
steps.what: PF would be added to <tenant-b> the way AIC already is: an IdP object plus a sign-on policy on the federation app. PF authenticates; PingOne takes the identity. Not done yet, and a write to ask about first.
steps.why: This brings the PF user in. It does not carry PF claims through to Cedar.

steps.title: The token Cedar sees is Privilege's
steps.what: <tenant-a> issues the token with its own scopes. PF scopes appearing in context.token.scopes is untested; assume they do not.
steps.why: Protect on identity and groups, not on a PF scope, until a live call proves otherwise.

steps.title: The caller becomes a Privilege principal
steps.what: The gateway matches the caller to a Privilege user by email alias and loads that user's groups. Its log reports the registry: 4 users (+4 email aliases), 4 agents, 1 group, 112 resources.
steps.why: Group rules only work for people who exist in the Privilege directory.

steps.title: Cedar decides
steps.what: Active AI policies run on every call. The vocabulary is fixed: app, tool, arguments, token scopes, agent scopes, group, named agent, approval count. There is no raw claims object and no act or ID-JAG hook.
steps.why: A rule can only name attributes the engine exposes.

steps.title: Allowed calls reach the tool
steps.what: A refusal logs mcp_policy_denied. A hold logs mcp_policy_approval_required and opens an approval; the client retries after it is approved. Policies created as Candidate never enforce until set to Active.
steps.why: The hold-approve-retry loop is the same one proven on this door for SearchIndexTool.

steps.title: Route C: an agent presents a PF-issued JWT (designed, not set up)
steps.what: Register a Non-Human Identity of type OIDC Provider with the PF issuer, the agent's sub and PF's JWKS. Privilege generates the audience; PF must mint tokens carrying it. The access policy can then require claim values (dotted paths such as realm_access.roles) before a tool tier applies; with End user set to Resolved, the person named in the token becomes a Privilege user for group rules.
steps.why: This is the native claim gate. It lives in the access policy, not in Cedar; four sensor identities already prove the federation pattern on this tenant, but none exists for PF and no rule uses RequiredClaims yet.
